By [F1] the classes $[D(A)]$, $A\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda$, form a $\mathbb Z$-basis of $G_0(\mathrm{Rep}(H^\Lambda))$. The ingredients are the Schur-functor image theorem, exactness of $\pi$ and the double-centralizer/quotient description of [[thm-higher-level-schur-weyl-double-centralizer]]. These are the definitions and the standard-monomial basis theorem of [[def-dual-canonical-canonical-and-quasi-canonical-fock-bases]] and [[thm-standard-tableau-monomials-form-a-basis-of-the-highest-weight-fock-submodule]], together with the O-side dictionary $[L(A)]\mapsto L_A$, $[P(A)]\mapsto P_A$, $[T(A)]\mapsto T_A$ of [[thm-simples-projectives-and-tiltings-map-to-the-three-distinguished-fock-bases]]. **The O-side Grothendieck group is the integral Fock module.** At parameter one the parabolic category-O Grothendieck group is identified with the integral Fock module by $[M(A)]\mapsto M_A$, with $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(P,N)=\langle[P],[N]\rangle$ and $\langle P_A,L_B\rangle=\delta_{AB}$, by [[thm-the-parabolic-o-grothendieck-group-is-the-integral-fock-module]]; here $M(A)$, $L(A)$, $P(A)$ are the generalized standard, simple and projective objects of the genuine block $\mathcal O^\Lambda_\alpha$ of [[def-integral-parabolic-category-o-block-for-higher-level-schur-weyl-duality]]. The multiplicity $[N(B):L(A)]$ equals the Fock coefficient $d_{A,B}(1)$ of step 1.2 by the O-side multiplicity dictionary of step 1.3 and the Schur-image theorem of step 1.1. Hence $\Phi([S(B)])=\sum_{A\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda}d_{A,B}(1)D_A=S_B$, and the square submatrix on standard columns is unitriangular, so $\{S_B:B\in\mathrm{Std}^\Lambda\}$ is an integral basis; this completes (i). Consequently every basis vector $D_A$ is a rational linear combination of lowering words applied to the ground vector. Thus its weightwise duality identifies $V(\Lambda)^*_{\mathbb Q}$, interpreted as the direct sum of the costandard weight spaces, with the irreducible rational highest module. Hence $H/K\to Hg$, $b+K\mapsto bg$, is well defined and surjective. The exterior row basis has size $(d!/|J|)\prod_j(l-t_j+1)$. proof_steps.text: **The degree-one block.** For $I=\{0\}$, level $2$ and charge $(0,0)$ the degree-one cyclotomic quotient is $H^{(0,0)}_1=\mathbb C[x_1]/(x_1^2)$ by the level-two instance of [[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]], and it is already supported, so $B=\mathbb C[x]/x^2$ with $x=x_1$. Its radical is $(x)$ and its quotient is $\mathbb C$, so $B$ is local; the unique simple is $D_{01}=\mathbb C$ with $x\mapsto0$, the regular module $Y_{01}=B$ is its projective cover, and the regular composition series $0\subset(x)\subset B$ has successive quotients $D_{01},D_{01}$, giving $[Y_{01}]=2[D_{01}]$ in $G_0$. Every $B$-linear map $B\to D_{01}$ is determined by the image of $1$, so $\dim\operatorname{Hom}(Y_{01},D_{01})=1$. [given, algebra]

**The symmetric form on $B$ and self-duality.** The coefficient functional $\tau(a+bx)=b$ is a symmetrizing trace on $B$: it is linear, $\tau(uv)=\tau(vu)$ for all $u,v$ (both sides pick out the $x$-coefficient of the product), and its radical is zero because $\tau(x)\ne0$, so the associated form $\langle u,v\rangle=\tau(uv)$ has matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in the basis $(1,x)$, which is nonsingular. The anti-involution $\ast$ of [[def-degenerate-cyclotomic-hecke-algebra]] that fixes $x$ is the identity of $B$ here, so the form is generator-fixing, and it exhibits an isomorphism $Y_{01}\cong Y_{01}^{\circledast}$: the dual of the regular module with respect to the trace. This is the actual symmetric-algebra proof of cover self-duality, not an inference from self-duality of the head. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

**The degree-two block and its simple.** With $x=x_1$, $y=x_2$, $u=s_1$ the relations give $u^2=1$, $[x,y]=0$, $ux=yu-1$, $uy=xu+1$, $x^2=0$, and from $ux^2=0$ one gets $y^2=(x+y)u$, so the eight words $1,x,y,xy,u,xu,yu,xyu$ span the degree-two algebra; the models $(N,-N,-J)$ on $M_2(\mathbb C)$ with $N=E_{12}$ and $J$ the swap matrix, $(\epsilon,1+\epsilon,1)$ and $(\epsilon,-1+\epsilon,-1)$ on $\mathbb C[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2$ satisfy all relations, and $z=x+y$ is central with images $0,1+2\epsilon,-1+2\epsilon$; the Hermite polynomials $E_0=(1-z^2)^2$, $E_\pm=(1-E_0\pm(3z-z^3)/2)/2$ map to the separate factor identities. Each factor is generated by its images of $x,u$, so the homomorphism is onto the eight-dimensional product; the eight-word spanning bound proves that the span of the eight words is isomorphic to $M_2(\mathbb C)\oplus B_+\oplus B_-$ with $B_\pm=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/\epsilon^2$. The supported content cut at $2\alpha_0$ keeps the factor $M_2(\mathbb C)$; its simple module $\mathbb C^2$ has Gram matrix $J$, since $N^{t}J=JN$ and $(-J)^{t}J=J(-J)$, and it is self-dual and projective, so its projective cover is itself and its endomorphism ring is $\mathbb C$; degree $0$ contributes $\mathbb C$, and Hom-spaces between distinct content blocks vanish because they are different blocks. In particular the one-dimensional Fock weight vector $M_{11}$ is not the two-dimensional module $D_{11}$, and the degree-two projective cover has vector-space dimension $2$ and composition length $1$. Higher supported degrees vanish directly: in an all-zero-residue module on at least three strands, restriction to strands $1,2$ forces $x_2=-x_1$ and $x_1^2=0$ by the matrix factor. Since $s_2$ commutes with $x_1$, it commutes with $x_2$, and the recursion gives $x_3=x_2+s_2$. On either $s_2$ eigenspace this is $x_2\pm1$, which is invertible, contradicting nilpotence of $x_3$ at residue zero. Thus such a nonzero module cannot exist; applying this to the regular module proves the supported algebra is zero in every degree at least three. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

**The projected dual bases at parameter one.** In the tensor square at parameter one, $fM_{00}=M_{01}+M_{10}$, $f(M_{01}+M_{10})=2M_{11}$, and $e$ reverses these moves with coefficients $2,1$. Hence the ground constituent has basis $P_{00},P_{01},P_{11}$ as displayed, and its complementary trivial line is $M_{10}-M_{01}$. Projection along this line gives $D_{01}=\pi M_{01}=\tfrac12(M_{01}+M_{10})$ and fixes the endpoints. The normalized form is determined by $C_0(M_{00},M_{00})=1$, $e/f$ adjunction and orthogonality of distinct weights: $C_0(P_{01},P_{01})=C_0(M_{00},eP_{01})=2$, and $2C_0(P_{11},P_{11})=C_0(P_{01},eP_{11})=2$. Thus the mixed vector is $P_{01}=M_{01}+M_{10}$ of $C_0$-norm $2$, so the correct field dual is $D_{01}=\tfrac12(M_{01}+M_{10})$, and the endpoint vectors satisfy $P_{00}=D_{00}=M_{00}$ and $P_{11}=D_{11}=M_{11}$. proof_steps.text: In the degenerate quotient $x_1=m$ and $sx_2=ms+1$ give $x_2=m+s$. Hence the quotient is generated by $s$ with $s^2=1$. Conversely the assignments $x_1\mapsto m$, $x_2\mapsto m+s$, $s\mapsto s$ in $\mathbb C[s]/(s^2-1)$ satisfy both cross relations and commutativity, so they define an inverse to the map sending $s$ into the quotient. Evaluation at $s=1,-1$ identifies this algebra with $\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$, with inverse $(a,b)\mapsto(a+b)/2+(a-b)s/2$. In particular it has no nonzero nilpotents and has precisely the two one-dimensional simple modules $s=1,-1$. [F2, algebra, construct]

In the nondegenerate level-one quotient [F3], $X_1=Q$ and $X_2=Q\xi^{-1}T^2$, so it is generated by $T$. Conversely in the finite algebra $H_\xi(2)$ of [F1], $T^{-1}=\xi^{-1}(T-(\xi-1))$. The assignments $X_1\mapsto Q$, $X_2\mapsto Q\xi^{-1}T^2$, $T\mapsto T$ therefore give commuting units satisfying $TX_1T=\xi X_2$ and the cyclotomic relation. They define the inverse of the map from $H_\xi(2)$ into the quotient: both composites fix $T,X_1,X_2$ and their inverses. Hence the whole nondegenerate level-one rank-two quotient is exactly $H_\xi(2)$ for every $\xi\ne0$ and $Q=\xi^m$. This uses only the arbitrary-base affine and monic definitions, not a finite-$e$ theorem in the generic branch. [F1, F3, algebra, construct]

At $\xi=-1$, step 1.2 and [F1] give $H_{-1}(2)=\mathbb C[T]/((T+1)^2)$. Setting $\varepsilon=T+1$ identifies it with $B=\mathbb C[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)$, whose basis is $1,\varepsilon$ by division by the monic polynomial $\varepsilon^2$. Thus $\varepsilon$ is nonzero and nilpotent. Every $a+b\varepsilon$ with $a\ne0$ has inverse $a^{-1}-ba^{-2}\varepsilon$; those with $a=0$ are nonunits. Consequently $(\varepsilon)$ is the unique maximal ideal and is the nonzero radical. Every simple $B$-module is killed by $\varepsilon$: its image under this central operator is a submodule, and if the image were the whole nonzero simple module, its square could not vanish. The unique simple is therefore $B/(\varepsilon)\cong\mathbb C$. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

At rank two the limitation can be seen in an actual comparison formula. For $\xi\ne-1$ put $a=(\xi-1)/2$ and $b=(\xi+1)/2$. The map $T\mapsto a+bs$ respects [F1] because its values at $s=1,-1$ are $\xi,-1$; its inverse is $s\mapsto(T-a)/b$, since the quadratic relation implies $(T-a)^2=b^2$. At $\xi=-1$ this inverse is undefined and the specialized map sends $T$ to $-1$, killing the nonzero element $T+1$. This explicit generic comparison therefore does not specialize to an isomorphism. Other rank-two parameters can yield isomorphisms, including some roots of unity; that does not repair the universal assertion. [F1, step 1.1, algebra, construct]

The two algebras cannot be isomorphic: an isomorphism would send the nonzero square-zero element of step 2.1 to a nonzero nilpotent in the algebra of step 1.1. Their decomposition behavior also differs directly. The regular module of $\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C$ is the direct sum of its two simples. The regular module $B$ has the filtration $0\subset(\varepsilon)\subset B$ with both subquotients equal to its unique simple; it is indecomposable since an idempotent $a+b\varepsilon$ satisfies $a^2=a$ and $2ab=b$, forcing it to be $0$ or $1$. Thus even projective and simple classes cannot be identified across these two specializations by algebra transport. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 disprove the claimed universal algebra transport and step 2.2 exhibits its failure in a concrete comparison formula. The witness uses the entire rank-two algebras, with the degenerate full integer residue set; it is not a comparison with a supported cut retaining only the charge $m$. For a finite degenerate cut containing this entire example the root interval must contain $m-1,m,m+1$, since $x_2=m\pm1$ on its two simples. The calculation is choice-free and entirely over $\mathbb C$. It neither extends characteristic-zero canonical-basis identifications to positive characteristic nor replaces the separate root-of-unity comparison and grading theorems.
